summary: A note that users of UCSB's Remote Job Server could submit jobs that actually ran at UCLA-CCN's job service, without converting to the UCLA protocol. It lists the disadvantages, including extra control language, a UCSB batch account, and separate submit and retrieve steps. It builds on RFC 436 and 477.

eli5.summary: One university lets you drop off work with it, and it passes your work to a second university's computer, which is a bit slower and fiddly.

subtitle: UCSB users can submit jobs to UCLA's computer through a gateway service.

tldr.problem: Users at UCSB wanted to run jobs on UCLA-CCN's faster IBM 360/91 computer, but only UCLA's Remote Job Service (RJS) could access it, and learning UCLA's protocol was burdensome.
tldr.mechanism: UCSB set up a gateway that translates commands from UCSB's RJS interface into UCLA's RJS protocol. Users submit jobs using familiar UCSB commands; the gateway forwards them over the network to UCLA, which runs them and returns results.
tldr.outcome: UCSB users could access UCLA's computing resources without learning a new protocol, though the gateway added latency and required separate submission and retrieval steps.

today: RFC 490 describes a 1973 gateway service that is now obsolete. The concepts of gateway translation and cross-network job submission influenced later remote computing and distributed system architectures.

sections.title: Remote Job Submission via Gateway
sections.content: RFC 490 describes how users at UCSB's IBM 360/75 can submit jobs to UCLA-CCN's IBM 360/91 over the ARPA Network. UCSB's Remote Job Server gateway translates commands and data, allowing users to submit, execute, and retrieve output without directly using UCLA's RJS protocol. The gateway handles reading input cards, printing output, and punching results. Only UCSB reads and manages I/O; UCLA handles job scheduling, resource allocation, and execution.
sections.eli5: A middleman computer takes jobs in its own style and passes them to a faraway computer in the style that computer wants.

sections.title: Submission and Retrieval
sections.content: The process requires two phases. Submission uses the READ command to send job cards to UCLA in batches, with each batch terminated by a special delimiter to prevent following jobs from being sent by mistake. Retrieval uses PRINT or PUNCH commands, either for a specific named job or for all waiting output. Users can also query job status and manage output priorities. The current implementation requires separate submission and retrieval steps rather than a continuous conversation.
sections.eli5: First you send your job over, wait a while, then ask for the results back. You cannot talk to UCLA while your job is running.

sections.title: Commands and Parameters
sections.content: The gateway accepts several commands through JCL (Job Control Language): READ to submit jobs, PRINT and PUNCH to retrieve output (by job name or all waiting output), STATUS to query job progress, and TERMID to sign on as a named RJS terminal. Each command maps to a UCSB procedure called UCLARJS with parameters in the JCL PARM field. Error conditions include network outages, timeouts while waiting for output, and occasional bugs in UCLA's implementation that can lose small output files.
sections.eli5: Users type simple commands, like READ to send a job, PRINT to get results, or STATUS to check how it is going. Most problems come from network delays or the distant computer being busy.

references.text: Pickens, J. R., "The Remote Job Service", RFC 436, 1973.
